opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing is to respect the skepticism, because it's earned. Drug discovery scientists have seen a lot of waves of computational hype: docking, QSAR, early machine learning. Many of those tools looked great on retrospective benchmarks and then didn't move the needle on a real program. So when we walk in and say "we have an AI model," the default reaction is, "Okay, show me."

So we try to show, not tell. A few things matter a lot.

First, prospective validation over retrospective benchmarks. A medicinal chemist doesn't care much that you beat some leaderboard on a dataset that might overlap with your training set. They care whether the model makes a prediction before the experiment, and the experiment comes back the way the model said. We've put a lot of effort into wet-lab validation: designing binders, predicting structures, then testing them and reporting hit rates honestly, including the failures.

Second, meet them on their own targets. The most convincing moment is when a scientist brings a target they've been stuck on for a while, maybe a hard protein-protein interaction or something without a good crystal structure, and the model gives them something useful they couldn't have gotten otherwise. One real result on their own problem is worth more than any slide deck.

Third, be honest about where the models don't work. Scientists trust you more when you say, "Here's where we're confident, here's where the predictions get shaky, and here's how you can tell the difference." Calibrated confidence matters. If the model always sounds sure of itself, people learn quickly not to believe it.

Fourth, lower the friction to try it. That's part of why releasing models openly and making them easy to run matters to us. If a skeptical computational chemist can download the model, run it on their system over a weekend, and poke at it themselves, that does more than any sales conversation. Skeptics convert when they verify things themselves.

And finally, frame it as augmenting their judgment rather than replacing it. The best drug hunters have intuition built over decades. We're not trying to take that away. We're trying to give them a much bigger search space and better priors, so the experiments they choose to run are more likely to work. When people see it that way, as a tool that makes their lab time more productive, the conversation changes from "prove AI works" to "how do we fit this into our workflow."

r001.rationale: The candidate says a useful result on a scientist’s own target is especially convincing and describes prospective wet-lab validation as evidence of performance.

r002.rationale: The candidate proposes using a scientist’s own target, including one they have been stuck on, to see whether the model produces something useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is that you don't convince them. Not with a slide deck, anyway. Pharma scientists have been pitched "AI is going to transform drug discovery" for a decade now, and most of them have watched those promises evaporate. So the skepticism is earned. If you walk in and lead with benchmarks, you've already lost the room.

What actually works is letting them break it. Our best adoption has come from people who started out trying to prove the model was wrong. They'd take a target they'd been stuck on for two years, where they knew the structural biology cold, and they'd throw it at Chai to see it fail. And sometimes it does fail, and that's actually fine, because now they trust the model's behavior when it says something confident. But when it gets a binding mode right that took them months to resolve experimentally, that lands in a way no marketing ever could. They go back to their group meeting and say "look at this," and that's worth more than any sales call.

The second thing is being honest about where the model is weak. Scientists can smell overclaiming instantly. If you say "it predicts everything," they stop listening. If you say "it's very good at protein-ligand complexes in this regime, it's shakier here, and here's how to tell which is which," they lean in. We spend a lot of time on calibration for exactly that reason. A prediction with no confidence signal is almost useless to a medicinal chemist, because they need to decide what to synthesize next week, and that's real money and real time.

And then the last piece is meeting them inside their workflow. Nobody wants to learn a new tool just because the model is clever. If it drops into the pipeline they already run, and the outputs look like the things they already know how to read, the barrier basically goes away. The goal isn't for them to believe in AI. The goal is for them to make one decision a little faster or a little better, notice it, and come back.

r001.rationale: It says scientists are persuaded when Chai gets a binding mode right on a target they had struggled to resolve, prompting them to show colleagues.

r002.rationale: It describes scientists testing the model on targets they had been stuck on for years to see whether it succeeds or fails.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the scientific problem they’re trying to solve, rather than trying to convince them that AI is exciting. Scientists are right to be skeptical. A prediction that looks compelling on a screen isn’t the same thing as something that works in an experiment.

So I’d frame it as: what’s a question you care about, and can we help you test it? What would count as a useful result? Then let the experimental evidence drive the conversation. Be clear about where the model is useful, where it’s uncertain, and what still needs validation.

The goal isn’t for somebody to trust AI in the abstract. It’s for them to have enough evidence that this tool can help them make a better decision about what to do next.

r001.rationale: The candidate says experimental evidence should guide the conversation and help scientists make decisions, but does not specifically say that demonstrated performance on relevant targets can persuade them to adopt Chai’s models.

r002.rationale: It proposes testing a question scientists care about, but does not specify testing targets they previously struggled with.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start by respecting the skepticism. These scientists have spent years learning how difficult biology is, so showing them a beautiful predicted structure and saying, “Look, AI works,” isn’t enough.

The useful question is: what experiment are you trying to decide to run next, and can we help you make that decision? If the model helps you prioritize candidates or generate a hypothesis you can test, then there’s a concrete way to judge whether it’s useful.

And you have to be honest about where it fails. A prediction isn’t experimental evidence. I’d rather have someone understand the limitations and use the model appropriately than trust it because we gave a convincing demo. Ultimately, the goal is to earn their confidence through results in their own workflow.

r001.rationale: The response says usefulness should be judged through experiments and results in scientists’ workflows, but it does not clearly say that demonstrated performance on relevant targets can persuade them to adopt the models.

r002.rationale: It does not propose testing the models on targets that pharma scientists previously struggled with.
